case_name: Fortune Resources and Properties LLP v. Y.P. Goel and Associates and Anr.
citation: MA No. 105 of 2025, Chhattisgarh High Court, decided 21 August 2026
holding_summary: A complainant alleged an oral agreement to buy a shop in a Raipur commercial project for Rs. 75 lakh, with part payment later refunded after possession and a sale deed never materialised. RERA dismissed the complaint for want of a written allotment agreement and held it lacked jurisdiction; REAT reversed, holding the complainant was still an 'aggrieved person' and remanding for fresh consideration. The Chhattisgarh High Court, dismissing the builder's appeal under Section 58 of RERA, held that the term 'aggrieved person' under Section 31 of the Act and Rule 35 of the Rules is of wide amplitude, and the mere absence of a written allotment document or agreement does not by itself oust RERA's jurisdiction over a real estate complaint.
why_it_matters: Prevents developers from defeating a RERA complaint on a pure documentation technicality, and signals that buyers who paid on the strength of an oral or informal booking can still invoke RERA rather than being pushed into ordinary civil litigation.

case_name: N. Balakrishnan v. Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
holding_summary: The petitioner sought to quash a TNRERA order granting project registration over a Thiruneermalai, Tambaram property that he claimed to own. Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy held that TNRERA cannot adjudicate disputed questions of title while examining a project registration application, and that a party disputing ownership must approach the competent civil court; TNRERA may refuse registration only where the absence of title or an encumbrance is apparent on the face of the record.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that RERA project registration is not a judicial finding of clear title, so a person disputing a developer's ownership cannot rely on RERA proceedings to resolve the title question and must pursue a separate civil suit.

case_name: ASR Market Ventures Private Limited v. Fitship Private Limited & Anr.
citation: C.O. (COMM.IPD-TM) 93/2025, Delhi High Court, decided 31 August 2026
holding_summary: ASR Market Ventures (owner of FITPASS) sought rectification of Fitship's registered 'FITFEAST' mark and an interim injunction in a connected passing-off suit, claiming it had coined FITFEAST in 2017. Justice Jyoti Singh dismissed the rectification petition and refused the interim injunction, holding ASR's own records showed it had consistently promoted its business under the umbrella mark FITPASS, with only scant, non-source-identifying references to FITFEAST, so ASR failed to establish goodwill in FITFEAST as a standalone mark.
why_it_matters: Shows that merely coining or occasionally using a term alongside a dominant house mark is not enough to claim standalone trademark rights in it — a business must show the secondary mark was itself used to identify source before it can rely on that mark against a later, independently adopted registration.

case_name: M. Gagan Bothra v. Senthil Kumar
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai Bench
holding_summary: A financial creditor, M. Gagan Bothra, filed a Section 95 IBC application against Senthil Kumar as personal guarantor of the corporate debtor, PRC International Hotels Private Limited. Senthil Kumar resisted the petition partly on the ground that he resided abroad. The NCLT, Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Sanjiv Jain and Technical Member Venkataraman Subramaniam), admitted the Section 95 petition, holding that the IBC does not restrict its applicability to personal guarantors based on nationality or place of residence, particularly where the guarantee was executed with a Chennai address and the underlying corporate debtor was based in Chennai.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that an NRI or overseas-resident personal guarantor cannot resist a Section 95 IBC petition merely by pointing to foreign residence or citizenship, giving financial creditors a clearer basis to pursue personal guarantors who have relocated abroad.

case_name: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth v. Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.
citation: (2026) ibclaw.in 1031 NCLAT; also cited as 2026 TAXSCAN (NCLAT) 226
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Principal Bench, New Delhi)
holding_summary: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth, a director and personal guarantor of M/s Veer Wires Private Limited, had guaranteed credit facilities extended by Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.; an arbitral award dated 23 June 2023 held the corporate debtor and its guarantors jointly and severally liable for Rs. 4.20 crore plus 14.5% interest. Sheth's Section 94 IBC application seeking his own insolvency resolution was ultimately dismissed by NCLT as an attempt to obtain an interim moratorium and obstruct the bank's lawful recovery and SARFAESI enforcement rather than a genuine bid at resolution and repayment planning. NCLAT dismissed Sheth's appeal, holding Section 94 applications must be pursued in good faith for actual insolvency resolution, not as a shield against creditor enforcement.
why_it_matters: Signals that NCLAT will scrutinise a personal guarantor's Section 94 application for bona fides and will not permit the interim moratorium it triggers to be used tactically to stall SARFAESI or other recovery proceedings — relevant to both guarantors and secured creditors litigating parallel recovery and personal-insolvency matters.

case_name: In Re: Cartelisation in the Supply of Tyres to Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation (Rekha Agencies & SS Marketing)
citation: Reference Case No. 01 of 2019, CCI order dated 21 August 2026
holding_summary: Acting on a reference concerning a 2013 Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation tender for tyre procurement, the CCI found that Rekha Agencies and SS Marketing — authorised dealers of JK Tyre & Industries Ltd. and CEAT Ltd. respectively — had exchanged commercially sensitive bid-price information by email before submission, with the prices ultimately quoted matching to the second decimal place, in contravention of Section 3(3)(d) of the Competition Act, 2002. The Commission imposed modest penalties on the two dealers (Rs. 1,29,901 and Rs. 2,13,274 respectively) but exonerated the tyre manufacturers themselves, including CEAT, finding no evidence the principal companies directed or participated in the bid-rigging.
why_it_matters: Shows the CCI will fix bid-rigging liability on an authorised dealer or distributor acting in a principal's name while declining to impute that liability to the manufacturer absent direct evidence of its involvement — a relevant distinction for manufacturers that route tender participation through independent dealer networks.

case_name: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
citation: APTEL, order dated on or about 28-29 September 2026, setting aside MERC order dated 30 May 2019
holding_summary: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. (SIIPL) operates wind power plants totalling 57.2 MW across Dhule, Sangli and Satara districts in Maharashtra, consuming the power captively and supplying surplus to third-party consumers through Open Access. During April 2016-March 2018, Open Access restrictions prevented delivery of generated power to SIIPL's intended consumers, causing over 3.67 crore units of surplus wind energy to be injected into the state grid instead; MERC rejected SIIPL's claim for compensation by an order dated 30 May 2019. APTEL set aside MERC's rejection and directed MERC to determine, together with applicable carrying costs, the amount payable to SIIPL by Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. for the surplus energy injected during the restricted period.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a captive generator is entitled to compensation for surplus energy injected into the grid when regulatory Open Access restrictions prevent its delivery to the generator's own consumers, reinforcing that a distribution licensee cannot retain the benefit of such injected power without payment.

case_name: Procure Logistics Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd.
holding_summary: Procure Logistics Services Pvt. Ltd., which had maintained a KYC-compliant current account with Axis Bank since 2011, sought to deposit demonetised Rs. 500 and Rs. 1,000 notes within the window permitted by the Government's November 2016 demonetisation notification. Axis Bank refused further deposits citing suspicion, despite the account being KYC-compliant and the deposits being supported by the company's audited financial records. The NCDRC held Axis Bank liable for deficiency in service, holding that the demonetisation notification did not empower a bank to unilaterally refuse deposits into a KYC-compliant account within the permitted window, and directed the bank to pay the complainant Rs. 3.19 crore with 6% simple interest from 30 December 2016 until payment.
why_it_matters: Confirms that during a government-mandated currency-exchange window, a bank cannot invoke generalised suspicion to refuse deposits into an account it has itself certified as KYC-compliant, giving businesses a clear deficiency-of-service precedent where a bank obstructs the exercise of a government-conferred right.

case_name: PVCON Engineering Co. v. CGST and Central Excise, Bhopal
citation: SLP (C) No. 28059 of 2026, Supreme Court, order dated 21 September 2026
holding_summary: PVCON Engineering, a road/construction contractor, received a penalty-only Order-in-Original dated 3 October 2024 (pursuant to a Show Cause Notice dated 26 July 2024 concerning alleged passing-on of irregular ITC without actual supply), and its Section 107 appeal was dismissed as time-barred. Challenging the Madhya Pradesh High Court's dismissal of its writ, PVCON argued the amended pre-deposit requirement for appeals before the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) could not apply to proceedings initiated before 1 October 2025. Justices K.V. Viswanathan and Arun Palli permitted PVCON to file its GSTAT appeal without the mandatory pre-deposit, expressly subject to the outcome of the pending SLP, and kept the jurisdictional challenge to the issuing DGGI officer open for adjudication.
why_it_matters: Gives taxpayers facing a penalty-only GST order issued before the 1 October 2025 pre-deposit amendment a concrete basis to seek interim relief from the pre-deposit condition when approaching GSTAT, pending a final ruling on the amendment's retrospective reach.

case_name: State of Odisha and Others v. Dhanurdhar Champatiray
citation: Orissa High Court, decided 21 September 2026 (Routray, J.)
holding_summary: Nine writ petitions challenged orders of District Judges, sitting as appellate authorities under Section 37(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The respondents raised a common preliminary objection that, since the Arbitration Act bars a second appeal against such orders (an appeal lying only to the Supreme Court), the writ petitions were an impermissible substitute for a second appeal. Justice B.P. Routray rejected the objection, holding that the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is not an appellate remedy and cannot be curtailed by a statutory bar on second appeals, though he confirmed that such supervisory jurisdiction over a Section 37 order remains confined to cases of egregious illegality, perversity or a patent lack of jurisdiction.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a party left without a further statutory appeal after a Section 37 order is not without recourse and can still invoke the High Court's limited supervisory writ jurisdiction, though only in cases of serious jurisdictional or legal error rather than as a routine further round of merits review.

case_name: Shivam Traders and Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. v. Madhusudan Vehicles Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: Shivam Traders, an NBFC, had received a long-term loan of Rs. 19.25 crore from Madhusudan Vehicles under a nine-year facility in 2019, and alleged the lender began pressing for premature repayment after only a year, prompting RBI complaints; Shivam Traders' civil suit for an injunction against premature recovery was rejected at the plaint stage, and its first appeal also failed. The Allahabad High Court dismissed its further appeal, holding that under Section 45QA of the RBI Act, 1934 read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, only the NCLT has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the premature repayment of a deposit or loan from an NBFC, and a civil court has no jurisdiction to grant an injunction restraining such recovery.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a borrower cannot use an ordinary civil suit or injunction to resist an NBFC's premature-recovery demand, and must instead raise any such dispute before the NCLT under Section 45QA -- relevant to any business financed by an NBFC that wants to contest early-repayment pressure.

case_name: M/s Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd. v. Haryana Power Purchase Centre & Anr.
holding_summary: In a dispute over the generic tariff applicable to Siwana's 5 MW solar project in Haryana, the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission had directed the Haryana Power Purchase Centre to pay a higher tariff of Rs. 6.44/kWh. APTEL, per Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat, set aside that direction, holding the applicable-tariff question had already been finally decided in earlier proceedings between the same parties and could not be reopened, and restored Rs. 5.68/kWh as the binding rate for the project.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that a solar generator or distribution utility cannot relitigate a tariff question already settled in a prior round of proceedings between the same parties, underscoring the finality of earlier SERC/APTEL tariff determinations in long-term power purchase arrangements.
